etymologies.etymologyHTML: Alteration (due to give) of Middle English foryiven, forȝiven, from Old English forġiefan (“to forgive, to give”), from Proto-West Germanic *frageban, from Proto-Germanic *fragebaną (“to give away; give up; release; forgive”), equivalent to for- +‎ give (etymologically for- + yive). Cognate with Scots forgeve, forgif, forgie (“to forgive”), West Frisian ferjaan (“to forgive”), Dutch vergeven (“to forgive”), German vergeben (“to forgive”), Icelandic fyrirgefa (“to forgive”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To pardon (someone); to waive any negative feeling towards or desire for punishment or retribution against.
(transitive) To pardon for (something); to waive any negative feeling over or retribution for.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Prologue:
quote.text: Forgive these wild and wandering cries,⁠Confusions of a wasted youth;⁠Forgive them where they fail in truth,And in thy wisdom make me wise.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To waive or remit (a debt), to absolve from payment or compensation of.

quote.citation: a. 1768, Laurence Sterne, Joseph's History considered; - Forgiveness of Injuries (sermon)
quote.text: The brave know only how to forgive  […] A coward never forgave; it is not in his nature.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To look past; to look beyond.
(transitive) To redeem; to offset the bad effects of something.

quote.citation: 2015, Todd in the Shadows, The Top Ten Best Hit Songs of 2014:
quote.text: Okay, a good hook forgives everything.
